subject: math
cluster: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
skillName: Data Plots on the Number Line
description: Students represent a univariate quantitative data set with the three plot types built on the real number line: dot plots, histograms, and box plots. For dot plots they place one mark above each value on a number-line scale and read frequencies back off the stack heights. For histograms they group continuous data into equal-width intervals (bins), tally the frequency in each bin, and read or build bars whose heights are those frequencies, attending to the bin boundary convention (a value on a boundary belongs to one bin only). For box plots they compute the five-number summary (minimum, first quartile $Q_1$, median, third quartile $Q_3$, maximum), locate those five values on a number-line scale, draw the box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with a line at the median and whiskers to the extremes, and compute the interquartile range $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$. Students choose an appropriate display for a given data set and read values, counts, and proportions back off each display.
subSkills: Build and read a dot plot: stack one dot per data value over a number-line scale and recover the frequency of any value from the stack height
Order a data set and find the five-number summary: minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum
Compute the median of a data set with an odd or an even number of values
Compute the quartiles $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ as the medians of the lower and upper halves
Compute the interquartile range $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$ and the range $\text{max}-\text{min}$
Construct a box plot by plotting the five-number summary on a number-line scale with box and whiskers
Read counts and the five-number summary back off an existing box plot
Group quantitative data into equal-width intervals and tally frequencies for a frequency table
Construct and read a histogram, applying the boundary convention so each value is counted in exactly one bin
Choose an appropriate display (dot plot, histogram, or box plot) for a given data set and purpose

problemArchetypes.name: Read a dot plot
problemArchetypes.example: A dot plot of quiz scores shows stacks of heights $1,3,4,2$ over the values $6,7,8,9$. How many students scored at least $8$? Add the stacks at $8$ and $9$: $4+2=6$ students.

problemArchetypes.name: Build the five-number summary
problemArchetypes.example: For the data $4,7,8,8,10,12,15$ find the five-number summary. Ordered, $n=7$: minimum $4$, median $8$, lower half $4,7,8$ gives $Q_1=7$, upper half $10,12,15$ gives $Q_3=12$, maximum $15$.

problemArchetypes.name: Compute the IQR
problemArchetypes.example: A data set has $Q_1=23$ and $Q_3=41$. Find the interquartile range: $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=41-23=18$.

problemArchetypes.name: Construct a box plot
problemArchetypes.example: Given the data $5,6,8,9,11,12,14,18$ (with $n=8$), find the five-number summary and describe the box plot. Median $=\dfrac{9+11}{2}=10$, $Q_1=\dfrac{6+8}{2}=7$, $Q_3=\dfrac{12+14}{2}=13$, minimum $5$, maximum $18$; the box runs from $7$ to $13$ with a line at $10$ and whiskers to $5$ and $18$.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a box plot
problemArchetypes.example: A box plot has minimum $12$, $Q_1=18$, median $25$, $Q_3=30$, maximum $40$. What fraction of the data lies between $18$ and $30$? About $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the data lies in the box (from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$).

problemArchetypes.name: Build a frequency table for a histogram
problemArchetypes.example: Group the data $2,4,5,7,9,11,12,14,15,19$ into bins of width $5$ starting at $0$ ($[0,5),[5,10),[10,15),[15,20)$). The frequencies are $2,2,3,3$, using the convention that a value on the right boundary belongs to the next bin.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a histogram
problemArchetypes.example: A histogram of ages has bars of heights $4,7,5,2$ over the bins $[10,20),[20,30),[30,40),[40,50)$. How many people are younger than $30$? Add the first two bars: $4+7=11$.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose an appropriate display
problemArchetypes.example: A teacher has the test scores of $120$ students and wants to show the overall shape and spread. A histogram (or box plot) is appropriate because the data set is large; a dot plot would require $120$ stacked dots and become unreadable.

Easy.description: Direct reads and single-step counts off a fully described display, or a five-number summary for a small data set with an odd count where the quartiles land on actual data values. tier1 lives here and ramps into Medium.
constraints: Dot-plot and histogram items state every stack height or bar height in the prompt; the task is to add a few of them
Five-number-summary items use an odd $n$ between $5$ and $9$ so the median is a single middle value and quartiles are the middles of clean halves
All data values are positive whole numbers with $\text{max}\le 30$
IQR and range tasks give $Q_1,Q_3$ (or min, max) directly and ask for one subtraction

Medium.description: A full five-number summary for an even-count data set where the median and quartiles are averages of two values, building a frequency table from raw data with the boundary convention, or computing the IQR after first finding the quartiles. tier1 ends here and tier2 begins here.
constraints: Even $n$ between $8$ and $12$, so the median is $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ and at least one quartile is an average of two values
Histogram items require grouping raw data into equal-width bins and applying the boundary rule (value on a boundary counts in exactly one bin)
Data values may reach the hundreds and a quartile or median may be a value ending in $.5$
Box-plot construction requires computing the five-number summary first, not just plotting given values

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning that chains the summary with interpretation or a follow-up: comparing two distributions, reasoning about the percent of data in a region of a box plot, working backward from a display to a missing value or count, or justifying a choice of display. tier2 lives here.
constraints: Reason about proportions of data using the quartile rule (each whisker and each box half holds about $25\%$ of the data)
Work backward: given a box plot or partial summary, recover a missing data value, an unknown frequency, or the original sample size
Compare two data sets' box plots or histograms and justify which has the greater median, range, or IQR in a sentence
Justify the most appropriate display for a described data set, citing size, shape, or the need to show individual values

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student finds the five-number summary without first ordering the data
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $12,4,8,15,7,10,8$ takes the median as the physical middle entry $15$ instead of ordering to $4,7,8,8,10,12,15$ and reading the true median $8$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the range with the interquartile range
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a set with min $4$, $Q_1=7$, $Q_3=12$, max $15$ reports the IQR as $15-4=11$ instead of $Q_3-Q_1=12-7=5$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student includes the median value in both halves when finding quartiles for an odd-count set
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $4,7,8,8,10,12,15$ uses the lower half $4,7,8,8$ and gets $Q_1=\dfrac{7+8}{2}=7.5$ instead of excluding the median and using $4,7,8$ to get $Q_1=7$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student double-counts a value that sits exactly on a histogram bin boundary
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For data $5,5,10$ with bins $[0,5),[5,10),[10,15)$ counts the value $5$ in both the first and second bins, reporting frequencies $1,3,1$ instead of $0,2,1$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reads dot-plot stack height as the data value rather than the frequency
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a dot plot with a stack of height $4$ over the value $8$ reports that the value is $4$ instead of reporting that $4$ students scored $8$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes each region of a box plot contains an equal length rather than an equal share of the data
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a box plot with min $12$, $Q_1=18$, median $25$, $Q_3=30$, max $40$ claims the long left whisker ($12$ to $18$) holds more data than the short box, instead of recognizing each quarter holds about $25\%$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student takes the median of an even-count set as one of the two middle values instead of their average
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $5,6,8,9,11,12,14,18$ reports the median as $9$ (or $11$) instead of $\dfrac{9+11}{2}=10$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a dot plot for a large data set where it becomes unreadable
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Recommends a dot plot to display the test scores of $120$ students instead of a histogram or box plot suited to large data
